Vexed has two distinct meanings depending on how it is used. Both are important, and knowing both will make you fully fluent with this word.
Meaning 1 — Feeling annoyed, troubled, or frustrated

When a person is described as vexed, they are feeling a kind of irritated annoyance — the sort of feeling you get when something keeps bothering you, going wrong, or refusing to be resolved.

It is not rage or fury. It is not a brief flash of irritation either. It sits somewhere in between: a persistent, nagging frustration — the kind that builds when you are dealing with something troublesome that won't go away, or when someone keeps doing something that gets on your nerves.

Think of it this way: if someone keeps interrupting you while you are trying to work, and you have asked them to stop more than once, the feeling you end up with — that tight, fed-up, bothered feeling — is exactly what vexed describes.

Examples:

  • She was vexed by the constant noise from the street outside.
  • He grew increasingly vexed when his computer crashed for the third time.
  • The teacher was vexed that no one had done the assignment.

Notice that in all these cases, the feeling has a cause, and that cause tends to be something the person finds difficult, unfair, or hard to control. This is key — vexed almost always implies something is making you feel this way, not just a mood you woke up with.

How strong is the emotion?
On a scale of emotional intensity, vexed is moderately strong — clearly more than mildly annoyed, but not as overwhelming as furious or enraged. It carries a sense of weariness too, like you have been patient but are running low on patience.
Meaning 2 — A vexed question / vexed issue / vexed problem

This is a completely different use of the word, but just as common and important. When vexed is used to describe a topic, question, or issue (not a person), it means the topic is difficult, deeply complicated, and long-debated — something that has been argued about for a long time without anyone arriving at a clear or agreed-upon answer.

The logic connecting this to Meaning 1 is intuitive: a vexed question is one that vexes (troubles, frustrates) the people who try to answer it.

Examples:

  • Immigration has long been a vexed issue in many democracies.
  • The vexed question of how to fairly distribute wealth has no simple answer.
  • Scientists continue to debate the vexed problem of consciousness.

A "vexed question" is not just a hard question — it is specifically one that causes disagreement, resists easy answers, and tends to generate ongoing debate. When you hear this phrase, it signals: this is a thorny, contested, complicated matter — tread carefully.

Vexed is a slightly formal word. You are more likely to encounter it in books, essays, journalism, formal speeches, or careful writing than in casual everyday speech. In ordinary conversation, people might instead say annoyed, frustrated, or bothered — but vexed is chosen when the writer or speaker wants to convey something a bit more precise or slightly literary in tone.

It is also notably common in British English, though it is by no means absent from American English.
How it differs from similar words

• Annoyed is the closest everyday equivalent for Meaning 1, but vexed implies a deeper, more sustained frustration — and a stronger sense that something is causing the feeling.
  • Frustrated is similar but leans more toward the feeling of being blocked or unable to succeed. Vexed is more about being troubled and bothered.
  • Irritated is milder — a small, quick reaction. Vexed is heavier and more lasting.

UseWhat it means
Describing a personFeeling persistently annoyed, troubled, and frustrated by something
Describing an issue/questionDeeply complicated, long-debated, and difficult to resolve

The single word that sits at the heart of vexed in both its uses is trouble — either you are troubled (Meaning 1), or the subject itself is troubling to everyone who touches it (Meaning 2).
